claim: SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern have emerged during the evolutionary history of SARS-CoV-2 with humans since late 2019, including the D614G mutation in Spring 2020, variant Alpha in Fall 2020, and Delta in Spring 2021.
source: During the short evolutionary history of SARS-CoV-2 with humans, since the host shift in late 2019, several selected mutations and combinations of mutations (variants) have emerged: for example, the D614G mutation in Spring 2020 (Volz et al., 2021a), the variant Alpha in Fall 2020 (B.1.1.7), and Delta in Spring 2020 (B.1.617.2).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published work (Volz et al., 2021a).

claim: Variant Alpha was first detected in England in September 2020.
source: Variant Alpha, first detected in England in September 2020, rapidly rose in frequency in October 2020 in England and spread to multiple countries, causing important rebounds of the epidemic (Volz et al., 2021b; Davies et al., 2021; Borges et al., 2021; Washington et al., 2021; Gaymard et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Variant Alpha rapidly rose in frequency in October 2020 in England and spread to multiple countries, causing important rebounds of the epidemic.
source: Variant Alpha, first detected in England in September 2020, rapidly rose in frequency in October 2020 in England and spread to multiple countries, causing important rebounds of the epidemic (Volz et al., 2021b; Davies et al., 2021; Borges et al., 2021; Washington et al., 2021; Gaymard et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by multiple citations.

claim: The Delta variant became dominant in many parts of the world, leading to new surges in infections and hospitalizations in 2021.
source: Later on, the Delta variant became dominant in many parts of the world, leading to new surges in infections and hospitalizations in 2021.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and reflects established knowledge about the Delta variant's impact.

claim: The R advantage of the Alpha variant was estimated to decline from +89 to +54% from December to mid-January in the United Kingdom.
source: For example, in the United Kingdom, the R advantage of the Alpha variant was estimated to decline from +89 to +54% from December to mid-January.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text, describing observed variability in R advantage estimates.

claim: Estimates of R advantage of Alpha and Delta across countries exhibit substantial variability.
source: Estimates of R advantage of Alpha and Delta across countries also exhibit substantial variability (Campbell et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation.

claim: The exponential growth rate of an emerging variant depends on both the effective reproduction number and the generation time distribution.
source: However, the growth rate of an emerging variant depends not only on the effective reproduction number but also on the generation time distribution.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and represents a fundamental epidemiological principle.

claim: Natural selection is expected to act on the full infectivity profile, which combines both R and the generation time.
source: Natural selection is therefore expected to act on the full infectivity profile, which combines both R and the generation time.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and represents a logical inference from evolutionary principles.

claim: Selection on variants with larger R increases with levels of transmission in the community.
source: It is known that selection on a variant with larger R increases with levels of transmission in the community.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and represents established knowledge in epidemiology.

claim: Variants conferring earlier transmission are more strongly favored when the historical strains have fast epidemic growth.
source: We additionally show that variants conferring earlier transmission are more strongly favored when the historical strains have fast epidemic growth, while variants conferring later transmission are more strongly favored when historical strains have slow or negative growth.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the abstract as a key finding of the study.

claim: Variants conferring later transmission are more strongly favored when historical strains have slow or negative growth.
source: We additionally show that variants conferring earlier transmission are more strongly favored when the historical strains have fast epidemic growth, while variants conferring later transmission are more strongly favored when historical strains have slow or negative growth.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the abstract as a key finding of the study.

claim: Alpha confers a +54% [95% CI, 45–63%] R advantage compared to previous strains.
source: Applied to data for the Alpha and Delta variants in England and in Europe, we find that Alpha confers a+54% [95% CI, 45–63%] R advantage compared to previous strains, and Delta +140% [98–182%] compared to Alpha, and mean generation times are similar to historical strains for both variants.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the abstract and represents a key finding from data analysis.

claim: Delta confers a +140% [95% CI, 98–182%] R advantage compared to Alpha.
source: Applied to data for the Alpha and Delta variants in England and in Europe, we find that Alpha confers a+54% [95% CI, 45–63%] R advantage compared to previous strains, and Delta +140% [98–182%] compared to Alpha, and mean generation times are similar to historical strains for both variants.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the abstract and represents a key finding from data analysis.

claim: Mean generation times are similar to historical strains for both Alpha and Delta variants.
source: Applied to data for the Alpha and Delta variants in England and in Europe, we find that Alpha confers a+54% [95% CI, 45–63%] R advantage compared to previous strains, and Delta +140% [98–182%] compared to Alpha, and mean generation times are similar to historical strains for both variants.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the abstract and represents a key finding from data analysis.

claim: A variant with a shorter mean generation time is selected for in a growing epidemic because it produces the same number of secondary infections in a shorter time.
source: A variant with a shorter mean generation time is selected for in a growing epidemic because it produces the same number of secondary infections in a shorter time, while the same variant is counter-selected in a declining epidemic (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1C showing the selection coefficient as a function of transmission.

claim: A variant with a shorter mean generation time is counter-selected in a declining epidemic.
source: A variant with a shorter mean generation time is selected for in a growing epidemic because it produces the same number of secondary infections in a shorter time, while the same variant is counter-selected in a declining epidemic (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1C.

claim: A variant with a larger standard deviation in generation time is always selected for because it enjoys both an excess of early secondary infections and late secondary infections compared to historical strains.
source: A variant with a larger standard deviation (sd) in generation time is always selected for because it enjoys both an excess of early secondary infections and late secondary infections compared to historical strains.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and represents a theoretical finding from the model.

claim: In a growing epidemic, more individuals have been infected recently and there is a greater advantage to early transmission.
source: Generally, in a growing epidemic, more individuals have been infected recently and there is a greater advantage to early transmission, while in a declining epidemic, more individuals have late time since infection and therefore strains that transmit at later times have a greater advantage.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and represents a logical inference from demographic principles.

claim: In a declining epidemic, more individuals have late time since infection and therefore strains that transmit at later times have a greater advantage.
source: Generally, in a growing epidemic, more individuals have been infected recently and there is a greater advantage to early transmission, while in a declining epidemic, more individuals have late time since infection and therefore strains that transmit at later times have a greater advantage.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and represents a logical inference from demographic principles.

claim: At the level of transmission where R_H = 1/(1+δ₁), the distribution of time since infection is uniform and therefore the infectivity profile does not matter for the selection of the variant.
source: At this level of transmission, the distribution of time since infection is uniform—all ages of infection are equally represented—and therefore the infectivity profile does not matter for the selection of the variant.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and represents a theoretical finding from the model.

claim: Variants with the same reproduction number but distinct generation time distributions can exhibit a variety of epidemiological and frequency dynamics in the context of progressive decline of levels of transmission.
source: In the context of progressive decline of levels of transmission, variants with the same reproduction number but distinct generation time distributions can exhibit a variety of epidemiological and frequency dynamics (Figure 2A and C).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2A and C showing simulation results.

claim: The epidemiological dynamics (daily number of variant cases) are strongly affected by the generation time distribution of the variant.
source: The epidemiological dynamics, that is the daily number of variant cases, are also strongly affected by the generation time distribution of the variant (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2A showing simulation results.

claim: Frequency trajectories can be non-monotonous: a variant with shorter mean generation time could be selected, increase in frequency, but then decline in frequency as transmission declines.
source: Frequency trajectories can be non-monotonous: a variant with shorter mean generation time could be selected, increase in frequency, but then decline in frequency as transmission declines (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2C showing simulation results.

claim: The R advantage was almost always precisely inferred even with small sample size and small variability in effective reproduction number in the simulation study.
source: The R advantage was almost always precisely inferred even with small sample size and small variability in effective reproduction number (Figure 3, left panels).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3 showing simulation results.

claim: The relative mean generation time was well inferred only for a large sample size and large variability in effective reproduction number in the simulation study.
source: In contrast, the relative mean generation time was well inferred only for a large sample size and large variability in effective reproduction number (Figure 3, right panel).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3 showing simulation results.

claim: For small sample sizes, grouping data by week (instead of by days, for the same duration) improves inference of the relative mean generation time.
source: For such small sample sizes, grouping data by week (instead of by days, for the same duration) improves inference (Figure 3, green points).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3 showing simulation results.

claim: The temporal lag between infections and recorded cases does not affect the accuracy of inference.
source: The lag does not affect the accuracy of inference (compare with Figure 3), as expected since the time series of number of detected cases and variant frequency share the same lag with infections.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by comparison with Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mismatch between modeling assumption and the true generation time distribution led to a small overestimation of the relative mean generation time.
source: This mismatch between modeling assumption and the true generation time distribution led to a small overestimation of the relative mean generation time (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2 showing simulation results.

claim: In England, the frequency of the Alpha variant could be quickly inferred because some of the PCR tests for SARS-CoV-2 detection presented a 'S gene target failure' (SGTF) caused by the spike 69/70 deletion characteristic of Alpha.
source: In England, the frequency of the Alpha variant could be quickly inferred because some of the PCR tests for SARS-CoV-2 detection presented a "S gene target failure" (SGTF) caused by the spike 69/70 deletion characteristic of Alpha (Public Health England, 2021b).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Public Health England.

claim: The variant Alpha swept through from 0% to almost 100% frequency over 25 weeks in England.
source: The variant Alpha swept through from 0% to almost 100% frequency over 25 weeks; data were of very good quality for the whole period (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4 showing the frequency dynamics.

claim: The inability to reliably disentangle R advantage from mean generation time for Delta in England was linked to the small temporal variations in epidemic conditions compared to the previous period when Alpha was investigated.
source: This was linked to the small temporal variations in epidemic conditions in this short period of time compared to the previous period when we investigated Alpha (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Alpha variant had a R advantage of +54% compared to historical strains, and the Delta variant had a further R advantage of +140% relative to Alpha, assuming a mean generation time of 6.5 days.
source: In conclusion, we found that the Alpha variant had a R advantage of +54% compared to historical strains, and the Delta variant had a further R advantage of +140% relative to Alpha, assuming a mean generation time of 6.5 days.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text as a conclusion from the data analysis.

claim: There was no evidence of an altered mean generation time for Alpha and Delta variants.
source: There was no evidence of an altered mean generation time for these two variants.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text as a conclusion from the data analysis.

claim: Levels of transmission reflected in the reproduction number R(t), which depend on human behavior and interventions, change selection on different types of variants.
source: We investigated how emerging variants with distinct infectivity profiles may be selected. Our main finding is that levels of transmission reflected in the reproduction number R(t), which depend on human behavior and interventions, change selection on different types of variants.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text as the main finding of the study.

claim: In a context of high transmission and high growth rate ('fast' epidemic), most infections will be recent and it is more advantageous to transmit early.
source: In a context of high transmission and high growth rate ("fast" epidemic), most infections will be recent and it is more advantageous to transmit early.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and represents a key finding from the theoretical analysis.

claim: In a context of low transmission ('slow' or declining epidemic), infections will be older and it is more advantageous to transmit late.
source: Conversely, in a context of low transmission ("slow" or declining epidemic), infections will be older and it is more advantageous to transmit late.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and represents a key finding from the theoretical analysis.

claim: The selection coefficient on variants may increase or decrease with the transmission, and it can even be a non-monotonous function of transmission.
source: The selection coefficient on variants may thus increase or decrease with the transmission, and it can even be a non-monotonous function of transmission.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and represents a key finding from the theoretical analysis.

claim: The variation of the selection coefficient with transmission provides insight on both the R advantage and the infectivity profile.
source: A second important finding is that the variation of the selection coefficient with transmission provides insight on both the R advantage and the infectivity profile.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text as a key finding of the study.

claim: Some studies of within-host viral load dynamics suggested that individuals infected by variant Alpha could shed virus for a longer time, which may result in a longer generation time.
source: Some (but not all) studies of within-host viral load dynamics suggested that individuals infected by variant Alpha could shed virus for a longer time, which may result in a longer generation time (Kissler et al., 2021; Cosentino et al., 2022; Elie et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published studies.

claim: A cluster of Delta variant infections in China suggested a smaller mean generation time (2.9 days) and more pre-symptomatic transmission for Delta than early SARS-CoV-2 strains, but without good control.
source: A cluster of Delta variant infections in China suggested a smaller mean generation time (2.9 days) and more pre-symptomatic transmission for Delta than early SARS-CoV-2 strains, but without good control (Zhang et al., 2021); more controlled studies found on the contrary a similar generation time (Pung et al., 2021; Ryu et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published studies.

claim: More controlled studies found a similar generation time for Delta compared to early SARS-CoV-2 strains.
source: A cluster of Delta variant infections in China suggested a smaller mean generation time (2.9 days) and more pre-symptomatic transmission for Delta than early SARS-CoV-2 strains, but without good control (Zhang et al., 2021); more controlled studies found on the contrary a similar generation time (Pung et al., 2021; Ryu et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published studies.

claim: If the distribution of generation time is similar in Delta, the observed growth rates imply it is +140% more transmissible than Alpha, in line with the +70 to +200% estimated elsewhere.
source: If the distribution of generation time is similar in Delta as we infer, the observed growth rates imply it is +140% more transmissible than Alpha, in line with the +70 to +200% estimated elsewhere (Alizon et al., 2021; Blanquart et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to other studies.

claim: If the generation time of Delta had been 1 or 2 days shorter than the baseline (6.5 days), the estimated R advantage would drop to +106 or +77%.
source: If the generation time of Delta had instead been inferred 1 or 2 days shorter than the baseline (6.5 days), the observed growth rate would imply the estimated R advantage drops to +106 or +77%.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and represents a counterfactual analysis.

claim: The large R advantage of Delta with similar mean generation time makes it more difficult to control with interventions reducing transmission (such as social distancing) than if it had a smaller R advantage associated with a shorter mean generation time.
source: The large R advantage of Delta with similar mean generation time makes it more difficult to control with interventions reducing transmission (such as social distancing) than if it had a smaller R advantage associated with a shorter mean generation time.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and represents a logical inference about intervention effectiveness.

claim: Several papers have reported a varying selection coefficient across time or across countries.
source: Several papers have reported a varying selection coefficient across time (Roquebert et al., 2021b) or across countries (Campbell et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published studies.

claim: One possible explanation for variability in selection coefficient is that it changes with transmission because of differences in generation time distributions.
source: One possible explanation for this variability is that the selection coefficient changes with transmission because of differences in generation time distributions, which may explain non-monotonous frequency trajectories (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2C showing simulation results.

claim: At a given level of transmission, stronger selection on a variant also implies a larger incidence of the variant and therefore a larger burden on healthcare systems.
source: Evolution influences epidemiological dynamics: at a given level of transmission, stronger selection on a variant also implies a larger incidence of the variant and therefore a larger burden on healthcare systems (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2A showing simulation results.

claim: Measures to reduce transmission, although possibly increasing the selection coefficient, always result in reduced variant absolute growth rate and better control of the variant.
source: However, we emphasize that measures to reduce transmission, although possibly increasing the selection coefficient, always result in reduced variant absolute growth rate and better control of the variant.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and represents a key clarification about intervention effects.

claim: The framework only considers the impact of changing transmission on selection for variants and does not consider the impact of interventions shortening the distribution of generation time such as isolation of positive cases and contact tracing.
source: A first limitation of our framework is that we only consider the impact of changing transmission on selection for variants. We do not consider the impact of interventions shortening the distribution of generation time such as isolation of positive cases and contact tracing, which also potentially change over time (Kraemer et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text as a limitation of the study.

claim: Interventions that shorten the distribution of generation time (such as contact tracing and case isolation) would alter the selection coefficient differently, in particular would favor earlier transmission (shorter mean generation time).
source: These interventions would alter the selection coefficient differently, in particular would favor earlier transmission (shorter mean generation time).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and represents a logical inference about intervention effects.

claim: Vaccination is an important factor that could change selection for variants and is not considered in the framework.
source: A second important factor that could change selection for variants and is not considered in our framework is vaccination.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text as a limitation of the study.

claim: If a variant partially escapes vaccine immunity, rapid vaccination of the population will change the selection coefficient of the variant over time.
source: If a variant partially escapes vaccine immunity, rapid vaccination of the population will change the selection coefficient of the variant over time.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and represents a logical inference about vaccination effects.

claim: The framework assumes that the variability in growth rates across countries is solely explained by changing transmission, and that the R advantage and distribution of generation time are the same in all countries.
source: A third limitation, linked to the comparison across countries, is that we assume that the variability in growth rates across countries is solely explained by changing transmission. The R advantage and distribution of generation time are assumed to be the same in all countries.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text as a limitation of the study.

claim: The framework requires precise measure of variant frequency and varying levels of transmission over the timespan considered.
source: Lastly, our framework requires precise measure of variant frequency and varying levels of transmission over the timespan considered.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text as a limitation of the study.

claim: Infectivity profiles can sometimes be inferred with as little as a 10 days time series after a sharp decline in transmission.
source: Infectivity profiles can sometimes be inferred with as little as a 10 days time series after a sharp decline in transmission (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 3 showing simulation results.

claim: The simple framework makes minimal assumptions (exponential growth rate and stable age-of-infection structure) that proved robust when tested against a simulation model including more complicated features.
source: In spite of these limitations, our simple framework makes minimal assumptions (exponential growth rate and stable age-of-infection structure) that proved robust when tested against a simulation model including more complicated features (build-up of immunity, isolation of positive cases, explicit epidemiological dynamics in the context of changing transmission).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and represents a validation of the framework.

claim: The patterns of growth of the Alpha and Delta variants in England and Europe are compatible with mean generation times similar to historical strains.
source: We find that the patterns of growth of the Alpha and Delta variants in England and Europe are compatible with mean generation times similar to historical strains.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text as a conclusion from the data analysis.

claim: When the number of infected individuals grows exponentially at a constant rate r, the distribution of time since infection equilibrates to an exponential distribution with parameter r.
source: It is known that when the number of infected individuals grows exponentially at a constant rate r, the distribution of time since infection equilibrates to an exponential distribution with parameter r (Wallinga and Lipsitch, 2007).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to established work.

claim: The generation time of historical strains was assumed to be gamma distributed with mean 6.5 days and sd 4 days.
source: We assumed the generation time of historical strains was gamma distributed with mean 6.5 days and sd 4 days (Volz et al., 2021b).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation.

claim: The time to detection has mean 7.3 days, which is the sum of time from infection to symptom onset with mean 5.1 days and the time from symptom to detection with mean 2.2 days.
source: The time to detection has mean 7.3 days. It is the sum of time from infection to symptom onset with mean 5.1 days (distributed as log-normal with parameters 1.518, 0.472 [Lauer et al., 2020]), and the time from symptom to detection with mean 2.2 days (distributed as gamma with shape 0.69, rate 0.31 [Belloir and Blanquart, 2021; Lauer et al., 2020]).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published studies.
